paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents need useful representations of states when their environments are large or continuous. Training a deep network directly on the main task may not produce those representations. Auxiliary prediction tasks offer another way to shape the features, but the choice of prediction method raises a basic question: what information does it actually teach the network to represent?

This paper theoretically characterizes the state representations learned through temporal difference learning, a method that bootstraps predictions from other learned predictions. In the policy evaluation setting, the authors find that these representations differ from those learned by Monte Carlo and residual gradient methods for most environment transition structures. The learning rule therefore affects the features themselves, beyond how predictions are updated.

The authors examine how effective these different representations are for evaluating a policy and use the analysis to develop new auxiliary learning rules. They also compare the rules empirically with different cumulant functions, which define the signals being predicted, in four-room and Mountain Car environments. The contribution connects the mechanics of bootstrapping to the representations that auxiliary tasks produce.
icml-2023-bootstrapped-representations-i.tldr: The paper characterizes how temporal difference learning shapes state representations and uses that analysis to design auxiliary learning rules.

paragraphs: Once a dataset has been divided into clusters, a separate problem remains: explaining what distinguishes each group. This paper starts with an existing partition and constructs a geometric description around each cluster. Each description is a polyhedron, a region defined by combining linear boundaries, so cluster membership can be described through a collection of conditions on the data features.

The method explicitly optimizes for simpler descriptions, either by reducing the complexity of the polyhedra or by reducing the number of features they use. The authors formulate this choice as an integer program. Because there are exponentially many candidate half-spaces from which to construct the regions, they use column generation to search the candidate space.

For larger datasets, the authors first combine points into smaller groups and then construct descriptions around those groups. They report that this strategy performs better than subsampling the data. Against existing cluster description algorithms, the approach achieves improved description accuracy with competitive interpretability. The result shows how optimization can balance faithful explanations of an existing clustering with descriptions that remain manageable to inspect.
icml-2023-cluster-explanation-via-polyhe.tldr: The paper explains existing clusters using optimized polyhedra, improving description accuracy while retaining competitive interpretability.

paragraphs: Synthetic tables need to represent both individual columns and the relationships between them. Mixed-type tables make this difficult because continuous values and discrete categories have different structures. The paper focuses on the remaining difficulty of modeling discrete columns, even as generative models have become better at producing realistic-looking tabular data.

CoDi divides the work between two diffusion models: one handles continuous variables and the other handles discrete variables. The models remain connected because each receives conditioning information from the other during training. This arrangement gives each variable type a separate modeling process while allowing information about the other type to influence what it learns.

The authors further connect the two models using contrastive learning with negative sampling. This adds a training mechanism for coordinating the models beyond their exchange of conditioning information. Experiments across 11 real-world tabular datasets, with eight baseline methods, support the effectiveness of CoDi. The central contribution is a way to combine separate treatment of different column types with joint learning of their relationships, addressing both parts of the mixed-type synthesis problem.
icml-2023-codi-co-evolving-contrastive-d.tldr: CoDi synthesizes mixed-type tables using mutually conditioned diffusion models for continuous and discrete variables, further linked through contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Predicting how two molecules interact requires deciding which parts of each molecule matter for that particular pairing. Existing graph-based approaches model molecules through their atoms and interactions, but the authors argue that they tend to overlook the role of larger substructures, such as functional groups. Those substructures can be central to distinctive chemical reactions.

CGIB approaches the problem by identifying core subgraphs within a pair of molecular graphs. Its objective is to retain the smallest amount of information sufficient for the prediction task, with relevance determined by the other graph in the pair. This conditional information bottleneck allows the selected part of a molecule to depend on its interaction partner.

The authors argue that this partner-dependent selection reflects how chemically relevant substructures can change across interactions. They evaluate CGIB on multiple tasks using real-world datasets and report stronger performance than state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support using conditional substructure selection for molecular relational prediction, with the paired molecule helping determine which information should be preserved in the representation.
icml-2023-conditional-graph-information-.tldr: CGIB predicts molecular interactions by selecting compact, task-relevant subgraphs whose importance depends on the molecule they are paired with.

paragraphs: Policy optimization learns a decision rule by updating it using feedback from interaction. Delayed bandit feedback complicates this process: information about a chosen action arrives later, while the learner continues making decisions. This paper studies that challenge in adversarial Markov decision processes, seeking guarantees for a widely used family of reinforcement learning methods.

The proposed algorithm, Delay-Adapted Policy Optimization, achieves the first near-optimal regret bounds for policy optimization in tabular MDPs. Regret measures the performance shortfall relative to a comparison policy. The authors also state that their bounds may surpass the existing state of the art, which relies on less efficient methods. That comparison is presented as a possibility rather than an unconditional improvement.

The design extends beyond finite tables. Assuming a linear Q-function, the authors handle infinite state spaces and prove the first delayed-feedback regret bounds with function approximation. They also adapt the approach to deep reinforcement learning and demonstrate effectiveness on MuJoCo domains. These contributions combine a tabular theoretical result, a function-approximation result under a stated assumption, and an empirical deep-learning extension.
icml-2023-delay-adapted-policy-optimizat.tldr: DAPO provides near-optimal tabular policy-optimization regret bounds with delayed feedback and extends to linear function approximation and deep reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Molecular generators often produce candidates that closely resemble their training molecules. That tendency restricts exploration when the aim is to discover unfamiliar molecules with potentially better properties. This paper introduces MOOD, a diffusion-based generation method designed to move beyond the training distribution while still directing its search toward relevant molecular properties.

MOOD places an out-of-distribution control directly into the stochastic differential equation governing generation. A hyperparameter adjusts that control, which the authors describe as requiring no additional cost. To keep novelty connected to useful properties, the method also uses gradients from a property predictor to guide reverse-time diffusion toward higher-scoring regions.

The targeted properties include protein-ligand interactions, drug-likeness, and synthesizability. This guidance addresses the authors' concern that unfamiliar molecules alone may fail basic requirements for drug candidates. In experiments, MOOD explores beyond the training distribution and generates molecules scoring above those produced by existing methods and even the top 0.01% of the training pool. These findings concern the evaluated property scores and support combining exploratory generation with property-directed guidance.
icml-2023-exploring-chemical-space-with-.tldr: MOOD combines controllable generation beyond the training distribution with property guidance to produce novel molecules with strong evaluated scores.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces the numerical precision of a trained network for deployment on devices with limited resources. It avoids requiring a full training dataset or end-to-end training. A central challenge is deciding how to round weights while preserving model behavior, often by reconstructing the outputs of individual layers or blocks.

FlexRound introduces a rounding mechanism based on element-wise division. It jointly learns a shared quantization grid size and a separate scale for each pretrained weight. The derivatives produced by division allow weight values to influence updates to their corresponding scales. This lets the rounding process respond flexibly to differences in weight magnitude.

The authors evaluate the method across image classification, natural language understanding, and natural language generation under a per-tensor uniform quantization setting. They also report that reconstructing outputs block by block can efficiently quantize large language models with negligible performance impact relative to half-precision baselines in their experiments. The contribution connects a particular rounding parameterization to broad empirical evidence that post-training compression can preserve useful model behavior.
icml-2023-flexround-learnable-rounding-b.tldr: FlexRound learns division-based weight rounding and reports effective post-training quantization across vision and language tasks, including large language models.

paragraphs: Many neural-network approaches implicitly treat observations as statistically independent, while real datasets often contain clusters connected through time or space. This paper incorporates correlated random effects into deep neural networks to represent that dependence. The setting also concerns categorical features with many possible values, where a model must account for substantial group structure.

The authors propose optimizing a hierarchical likelihood, or h-likelihood, objective. They state that joint optimization provides exact maximum likelihood estimates for mean and dispersion parameters, together with best linear unbiased predictions of the random effects. The approach also supplies a computable procedure for restricted maximum likelihood estimation of dispersion parameters, addressing several statistical estimation tasks within the same framework.

A two-step algorithm enables online learning for the neural-network component. The authors contrast this with integrated likelihood, which does not decompose like commonly used neural-network losses. Numerical studies and analyses of real data demonstrate advantages of the approach. Its significance is the combination of explicit dependence modeling, the stated estimation properties, and a training procedure compatible with online neural-network learning.
icml-2023-h-likelihood-approach-to-deep-.tldr: The paper uses hierarchical likelihood to train neural networks with correlated random effects, providing stated exact estimation results and an online-learning procedure.

paragraphs: Transfer learning adapts a pretrained model to a new task, often by training additional classification layers when labeled data are scarce. In a machine-learning service, that training can involve private client data. This paper addresses encrypted training, extending beyond the encrypted inference that had been the focus of most earlier work in this setting.

HETAL encrypts client data using the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, allowing the training computation to operate on encrypted data. The method includes validation-based early stopping and achieves the accuracy of nonencrypted training in the reported evaluation. The authors present it as the first practical scheme strictly providing this form of encrypted training.

Two computational components support that result: an encrypted matrix multiplication algorithm and a precise softmax approximation with broader coverage. The matrix multiplication method is reported to be 1.8 to 323 times faster than prior methods. Across five benchmark datasets, total training takes 567 to 3442 seconds, remaining below an hour. These results provide concrete evidence for the practicality of the proposed encrypted transfer-learning procedure in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-hetal-efficient-privacy-preser.tldr: HETAL enables encrypted transfer-learning training that matches nonencrypted accuracy in its evaluation and finishes within an hour on five benchmarks.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships between entities. Inductive methods address entities absent from training, but many still assume that every relation type is already known. This becomes restrictive when a new graph introduces unfamiliar entities alongside unfamiliar relations. InGram is designed to generate representations for both at inference time.

The method constructs a second graph whose nodes are the relations in the original knowledge graph. Weighted connections in this relation graph describe affinities between relation types. InGram then uses both graphs, learning through attention how to aggregate neighboring embeddings into representations of entities and relations. This gives relation structure an explicit role in constructing representations for new graph elements.

Experiments compare InGram with 14 state-of-the-art methods across varied inductive learning scenarios, and the authors report that it outperforms them. The methodological contribution is the use of a relation graph to extend inductive embedding beyond new entities alone. The empirical findings support that design in settings where the kinds of relationships encountered during inference can also differ from those seen during training.
icml-2023-ingram-inductive-knowledge-gra.tldr: InGram uses attention over knowledge and relation graphs to embed previously unseen entities and relation types at inference time.

paragraphs: In a partially observable decision problem, an agent must act without directly seeing the underlying state. This hidden information can make learning statistically intractable even in otherwise simple settings. The paper asks what changes when the learner can obtain additional information after the fact, a situation motivated by applications including robotics and data center scheduling.

The authors define a hindsight observable MDP as a partially observable process whose latent states are revealed retrospectively during training. That assumption is central: the extra state information is available for learning, while the decision problem remains partially observable. They introduce algorithms for both tabular representations and settings that use function approximation.

The algorithms are provably sample-efficient with hindsight observability, including for some problems that would otherwise be statistically intractable. A lower bound also establishes that the tabular algorithm has optimal dependence on the numbers of latent states and observations. The result identifies a specific form of training-time information that can change learning difficulty, with an optimality claim tied to those two dimensions rather than every aspect of the algorithm.
icml-2023-learning-in-pomdps-is-sample-e.tldr: Revealing hidden states retrospectively during training enables provably sample-efficient learning in some otherwise statistically intractable partially observable problems.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket question asks whether highly sparse network initializations can still be trained successfully. This paper investigates whether that phenomenon extends to evolution strategies, which optimize without backpropagation. The authors establish the existence of such sparse trainable initializations and examine how their behavior differs from sparse networks trained through gradient descent.

They introduce an iterative pruning procedure based on signal-to-noise information that incorporates loss curvature when choosing what to prune. The method can uncover even sparser trainable initializations for black-box evolutionary optimization than for gradient-based optimization. The authors also find that the resulting initializations carry an inductive bias that transfers across different evolution strategies, related tasks, and even gradient-based training.

The paper additionally compares the local optima reached under different optimization methods and sparsity levels. Evolution strategies explore diverse, flat optima and, unlike gradient descent in the reported comparison, do not preserve linear mode connectivity across sparsity levels and independent runs. These findings make pruning a tool for studying learning dynamics as well as for discovering trainable sparse networks.
icml-2023-lottery-tickets-in-evolutionar.tldr: Highly sparse trainable initializations also exist for evolution strategies, with transferable biases and learning dynamics that differ from gradient descent.

paragraphs: Metagenomic binning groups assembled DNA sequences, called contigs, according to the genomes they belong to. The paper argues that leading methods leave useful evidence unused by concentrating on features of each contig separately. In particular, overlapping reads connect contigs in an assembly graph, and marker genes provide further information for distinguishing sequences from different genomes.

CCVAE learns contig representations with a variational autoencoder, then uses those representations for binning. Its main change is to constrain the learned representations using connectivity from the assembly graph. The model also incorporates marker-gene information. Representation learning therefore draws on both the sequences' individual features and auxiliary evidence about their relationships and genome distinctions.

Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show CCVAE outperforming the state-of-the-art techniques evaluated by the authors. The stated result supports bringing structural and marker information into representation learning before the binning step. This matters because contigs are connected pieces of biological evidence, and the proposed method gives those connections a direct role in how the sequences are represented.
icml-2023-metagenomic-binning-using-conn.tldr: CCVAE improves metagenomic binning by learning contig representations constrained by assembly-graph connections and informed by marker genes.

paragraphs: This paper studies scheduling when dependencies between jobs are hidden. The algorithm learns that a job exists only after all its predecessors have finished, leaving it unable to inspect the full dependency structure in advance. Strong impossibility results for classical competitive analysis motivate asking whether predictions can provide enough additional information to improve scheduling.

The authors investigate a learning-augmented setting in which predictions are available but carry no guarantee of correctness. They compare several ways of supplying predictions, including new models tailored to this scheduling problem and more general models from earlier work. This makes the form of information part of the research question, alongside the algorithm that uses it.

For different dependency topologies, the paper supplies algorithmic upper bounds and lower bounds on achievable performance. Together, these results organize which kinds of potentially erroneous information help and how they can support better scheduling algorithms. The analysis also improves traditional competitive-ratio bounds for existing algorithms. The contribution is thus a structured account of the value of predictions under hidden precedence constraints, including boundaries on what algorithms can achieve.
icml-2023-minimalistic-predictions-to-sc.tldr: The paper characterizes how different, potentially erroneous predictions can improve scheduling when jobs and their dependencies are revealed online.

paragraphs: Many generative models produce samples by numerically following a continuous trajectory defined through an ordinary or stochastic differential equation. Each step can require another neural-network evaluation, making sampling slow. This paper connects that computational burden to the curvature of the learned trajectories, which is directly related to the truncation error introduced by numerical solvers.

The authors focus on the relationship between the forward process and the geometry of the reverse generative process. Instead of keeping the forward process fixed, they train it to reduce the curvature of generative trajectories. Their training method does this without simulating an ODE or SDE, providing a way to change trajectory geometry without requiring such simulation during that optimization.

Experiments show lower curvature than previous models and reduced sampling costs while maintaining competitive performance. The reported findings support trajectory shape as a useful target for improving generation efficiency. The contribution is a method for learning the forward process so that the resulting reverse process is less costly to simulate, linking the model's construction to the numerical work required at sampling time.
icml-2023-minimizing-trajectory-curvatur.tldr: Training the forward process to reduce generative trajectory curvature lowers sampling costs while preserving competitive performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Unsupervised pretraining can help reinforcement learning agents use interaction data more efficiently. One approach learns state representations by predicting future states in a latent space from a large unlabeled dataset. However, these representations can collapse into a low-dimensional structure, leaving the model with fewer distinct feature directions than its representation could otherwise support.

The paper proposes a framework that combines causal prediction of future states with feature decorrelation. The predictive objective encourages the representation to capture information about what comes next. Decorrelation reduces dependence between latent features, aiming to increase the dimension of the latent manifold and address the collapse that can accompany predictive representation learning.

Extensive empirical studies show that the framework learns predictive representations without collapse and significantly improves the sample efficiency of state-of-the-art unsupervised representation methods on Atari 100k. The findings connect an internal property of the representation to downstream learning behavior. In the evaluated setting, maintaining a richer set of feature directions works alongside temporal prediction to make the pretrained representation more useful for reinforcement learning.
icml-2023-on-the-importance-of-feature-d.tldr: Combining future-state prediction with latent feature decorrelation prevents representation collapse in the reported studies and improves Atari 100k sample efficiency.

paragraphs: A policy's occupancy measure records how often state-action pairs are expected to be visited, with or without discounting. Two policies can share this measure even if they choose actions using different information. For countable spaces, a longstanding result says that, under mild conditions, a history-dependent policy's occupancy can be reproduced by a policy that uses only the current state.

This paper develops a general measure-theoretic treatment that extends occupancy equivalence to continuous MDPs. The technical challenge is to formulate and establish the result beyond countable state-action collections. The equivalence concerns expected visitation: it identifies when a memoryless randomized policy can reproduce the occupancy associated with a policy that depends on the history.

The authors also examine the boundary of the result. When occupancy is infinite, they show that nontrivial cases arise in which the equivalence fails. That qualification matters because the extension cannot be read as an unrestricted statement for every continuous decision process. The contribution both fills a theoretical gap and identifies infinite occupancy as a setting where the expected correspondence can break down.
icml-2023-on-the-occupancy-measure-of-no.tldr: The paper extends occupancy equivalence between history-dependent and memoryless policies to continuous MDPs while identifying failures when occupancy is infinite.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling chooses among uncertain options through randomized probability matching. Although it has strong performance and optimality results in several reward models, much of that theory concerns light-tailed distributions or one-parameter exponential families. This paper studies a different setting: Pareto rewards, which are heavy-tailed and have two unknown parameters.

The authors examine how the choice of probability-matching prior affects regret, the accumulated performance shortfall from learning which option is best. They prove that certain priors allow Thompson sampling to achieve an optimal regret bound. Other priors yield suboptimal behavior, including the Jeffreys and reference priors. A prior's noninformative status therefore does not by itself ensure the desired performance in this model.

A truncation procedure changes that outcome for Thompson sampling with Jeffreys and reference priors: the authors show that it can then attain the asymptotic lower bound. The results establish both successful and unsuccessful prior choices and a procedure that restores asymptotic optimality for the identified cases. Their practical message is that prior selection and truncation can materially affect Thompson sampling in two-parameter, heavy-tailed reward settings.
icml-2023-optimality-of-thompson-samplin.tldr: For two-parameter Pareto bandits, Thompson sampling's optimality depends on the prior, and truncation restores asymptotic optimality for Jeffreys and reference priors.

paragraphs: Language often appears inside a visual structure: a document layout, an illustrated page, a form, or an interface. Models for these settings have commonly used separate training recipes. Pix2Struct introduces a shared image-to-text pretraining approach intended to support a broad range of tasks in which understanding language also requires interpreting its visual surroundings.

The model learns to convert masked screenshots of web pages into simplified HTML. This objective connects visible text and visual elements with the structure represented in the page markup. The authors describe it as intuitively encompassing signals associated with text recognition, language modeling, and image captioning. The method also uses a variable-resolution image representation and places language prompts directly onto the input image.

After fine-tuning, a single pretrained model achieves state-of-the-art results on six of nine tasks spanning documents, illustrations, user interfaces, and natural images. These findings support screenshot parsing as a broadly useful pretraining task for visually situated language. The contribution combines a shared training objective with input mechanisms that accommodate variation in both image resolution and task prompts.
icml-2023-pix2struct-screenshot-parsing-.tldr: Pix2Struct learns visual language understanding by parsing masked web screenshots into HTML and achieves state-of-the-art results on six of nine evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Speech translation must connect acoustic inputs with textual outputs, despite the gap between those modalities. This paper addresses that gap during pretraining, allowing the translation model's architecture to remain unchanged. The authors first show that connectionist temporal classification, or CTC, reduces the modality gap by design and consistently improves final translation accuracy over cross-entropy pretraining in their comparisons.

Because CTC addresses only part of the gap, the proposed method combines it with optimal transport. A paired-encoder model processes acoustic and textual inputs separately while learning representations that are close in Wasserstein space. This gives pretraining an explicit way to bring the two modalities' representations together before speech translation training.

On CoVoST-2 and MuST-C, the method applied to a standard encoder-decoder Transformer achieves state-of-the-art performance in the no-external-data setting. It also performs on par with strong multitask systems trained with external data. Applying the pretraining method to those multitask systems brings further improvements. The findings show that alignment during pretraining can benefit both a standard translation architecture and more elaborate training systems.
icml-2023-pre-training-for-speech-transl.tldr: Combining CTC and optimal transport during pretraining aligns speech and text representations and improves translation without changing the translation architecture.

paragraphs: Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths from a single source in graphs that can contain negative edge weights. Its running time depends on the order in which vertices are examined as distance estimates are repeatedly updated. This paper treats that ordering choice as an opportunity to improve the algorithm using information from related problem instances.

The authors work within the algorithms-with-predictions framework, where auxiliary information guides an algorithm. They identify Minimum Violation Permutations as the key ordering problem and develop algorithms for it with strong approximation guarantees. They also provide formal lower bounds, pairing constructive methods with results about the limits of what can be achieved.

An empirical evaluation shows that the resulting approach can produce a significant practical speedup for Bellman-Ford. The findings connect a familiar graph algorithm's runtime to a separate permutation problem that can use evidence from similar instances. The contribution includes both a theoretical treatment of that ordering problem and experimental support for using the resulting orderings to reduce shortest-path computation time.
icml-2023-speeding-up-bellman-ford-via-m.tldr: The paper uses information from similar graph instances to improve Bellman-Ford's vertex ordering, with approximation guarantees and demonstrated practical speedups.

paragraphs: People can adapt their behavior after a classifier is deployed, changing the inputs on which it makes decisions. Strategic classification accounts for this by balancing predictive correctness with robustness to manipulation. The task becomes harder when the learner does not know which changes are available to each individual, since that structure determines the adaptations it needs to consider.

This paper introduces a batch-learning setting that uses unlabeled data from earlier rounds to estimate the manipulation structure. Information gathered during previous rounds therefore helps the learner understand which changes are feasible. The approach brings learning about user adaptations into the classification process instead of requiring that structure to be supplied beforehand.

The authors show that a classifier close to optimal in strategic loss can be learned in this setting despite the initial uncertainty about feasible manipulations. Their result does not require agents to choose a best response to the classifier; it only requires observed manipulations to be feasible. The contribution establishes a learning possibility under those conditions, relaxing both prior knowledge of the manipulation structure and the assumption of perfectly optimizing users.
icml-2023-strategic-classification-with-.tldr: The paper shows how unlabeled observations across batches can support near-optimal strategic classification without advance knowledge of feasible user manipulations.

paragraphs: Some learning problems have gradients that are expensive to compute, including problems in reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and adversarial training. This paper proposes using an expensive gradient computation to construct a cheaper surrogate objective in a target space, such as a model's output logits. Optimizing that surrogate supports multiple parameter updates from the same costly computation.

In the full-batch setting, the authors prove that their surrogate globally upper-bounds the original loss. It can be minimized locally using a black-box optimizer, and the resulting majorization-minimization algorithm converges to a stationary point. This provides a theoretical basis for substituting repeated surrogate optimization for repeated evaluations of the expensive gradient.

For stochastic optimization, the authors introduce SSO and interpret it as projected stochastic gradient descent in target space. That connection supports theoretical guarantees for convex objectives. The framework allows standard stochastic methods to construct surrogates and deterministic methods to minimize them. Experiments on supervised and imitation learning problems indicate benefits from target optimization and support SSO's effectiveness, complementing the distinct full-batch and convex stochastic guarantees.
icml-2023-target-based-surrogates-for-st.tldr: Target optimization turns expensive gradients into cheaper surrogate objectives that support multiple updates, with convergence results and empirical benefits.

paragraphs: Attention-based graph neural networks learn how much influence neighboring nodes should have during information propagation. Increasing depth raises particular difficulties for this mechanism. The paper investigates vulnerability to over-smoothed features and excessive smoothness in cumulative attention, examining how these phenomena affect the attention used across many graph-processing layers.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors show that various attention-based GNNs suffer from these problems. They then propose AERO-GNN, an architecture designed specifically for deep graph attention. The method provably mitigates the identified issues, connecting the architectural remedy to the same problems established by the analysis.

Experiments further show adaptive, less smooth attention functions and stronger performance at deep layers, including networks with up to 64 layers. AERO-GNN outperforms the baseline GNNs on nine of twelve node classification benchmarks. The results support the usefulness of deep graph attention when its specific smoothing problems are addressed. The claim combines a theoretical mitigation result with empirical improvements across most, rather than all, of the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2023-towards-deep-attention-in-grap.tldr: AERO-GNN mitigates smoothing problems in deep graph attention and outperforms baseline GNNs on nine of twelve node classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Cooperating successfully can require knowing something about other participants, but some details of their behavior may be irrelevant to optimal coordination. This paper asks how to distinguish the information that matters strategically from information that can be ignored. The goal is to identify the knowledge needed to coordinate optimally in cooperative games.

The authors establish a well-defined division between strategically relevant and irrelevant information. For dynamic games, they show that this distinction has a compact representation that can be computed efficiently using a Bellman backup operator. This turns a conceptual question about collaborator knowledge into a computational procedure for identifying what information matters.

They apply the algorithm to tasks in both standard and partially observable versions of Overcooked. Theoretical and empirical results show substantial efficiency improvements over the baselines considered. The contribution links optimal coordination to a compact account of relevant knowledge, with applications demonstrating how the account can be analyzed in interactive tasks. It provides a way to reason about necessary collaborator information without treating every observable behavioral detail as equally useful.
icml-2023-who-needs-to-know-minimal-know.tldr: The paper characterizes strategically relevant collaborator information and provides an efficient way to compute it for optimal coordination in dynamic games.
